{{Short description|Australian herpetologist (1930–1950)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Kevin Clifford Budden''' (27 September 1930<ref>{{cite web|url=http://acms.sl.nsw.gov.au/item/itemDetailPaged.aspx?itemID=946087|title=Catalogue listing (Kevin Budden papers, 1948-1950)|publisher=Library of New South Wales|access-date=16 January 2014}}</ref> – 28 July 1950)<ref>Mirtschin, P. (2006); "The pioneers of venom production for Australian antivenoms", in: ''Toxicon'', Vol. 48, p. 899-918. Retrieved [http://www.venomsupplies.com/assets/Pioneers-published-paper.pdf online], 17 June 2017.</ref> was an amateur [[Australia|Australian]] [[herpetologist]] and snake [[Hunting|hunter]]. Budden was the first person to capture a live [[taipan]] for [[research]] and died from a [[snakebite]] in the process of doing so. His work was instrumental in developing a taipan [[antivenom]].<ref name="BT20140116">{{cite news|url=http://www.brisbanetimes.com.au/queensland/snake-venom-keeps-its-bite-80-years-on-20140115-30v38.html|title=Snake venom keeps its bite 80 years on|last=Atfield|first=Cameron|date=16 January 2014|work=Brisbane Times|access-date=16 January 2014}}</ref>

==Early life==
After leaving school, Budden worked as a retail assistant in [[Randwick|Randwick, New South Wales]].<ref name="News19490119">{{cite news|url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article130240510?|title=Catches snakes as a hobby|date=19 January 1949|work=News|page=13|access-date=17 January 2014|location=Adelaide, South Australia}}</ref> At that time he joined the [[Herpetological society#Australia|Australian Reptile Club]] and began hunting snakes as a [[hobby]]. He built a snake pit and spent weekends in the bush collecting snakes.<ref name="BM1950 814">{{cite news|url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article49579411?|title=Taipan Victim's Many Snakebites|date=14 August 1950|work=Barrier Miner|page=8|access-date=16 January 2014|location=Broken Hill, New South Wales}}</ref> In 1948, he caught 59 snakes and was bitten five times.<ref name="News19490119"/>

==Taipan capture and death==
{{multiple image
 | total_width = 300px
 | image1 = Oxyuranus scutellatus first milked specimen MV 3.jpg
 | alt1 = Close-up of a preserved snake's face, scales reddish brown and eyes replaced with beads.
 | image2 = Oxyuranus scutellatus first milked specimen MV 2.jpg
 | alt2 = Preserved snake, pale brown, coiled inside a glass with preserving spirits on an empty background.
 | footer = The specimen captured by Budden in 1950, from whose venom the first taipan antivenom was made. Currently preserved in spirits and stored in the collections of Museums Victoria.
}}
In March 1950, Budden travelled to [[Queensland]] with two colleagues to capture a [[taipan]] for [[antivenom]] research.<ref name="BT20140116"/> The group had previously visited [[Cape York Peninsula|Cape York]] and the [[Northern Territory]] on a similar [[Quest|quest.]]<ref name="BM19490330">{{cite news|url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article48589228?|title=Leaving on snake hunt|date=30 March 1949|work=Barrier Miner|access-date=17 January 2014|location=Broken Hill, New South Wales}}</ref><ref name="Worker10490411">{{cite news|url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article71412051?|title=Snake Scalpers|date=11 April 1949|work=Worker|page=4|access-date=16 January 2014|location=Brisbane, Queensland}}</ref> On 27 July, Budden captured a {{convert|6|ft|adj=on}} taipan near [[Cairns]]. He carried the snake by hand, caught a ride from a passing [[truck]], and took the snake to another local snake catcher, where it was identified as a taipan. While attempting to bag the snake, Budden was bitten on his left [[thumb]] but successfully placed the captured snake in a bag. Extracting a promise from the [[truck driver]] that he would get the snake to someone who would transport it south to researchers, Budden was taken for medical treatment. Not having any antivenom for taipans, Budden was given [[tiger snake]] antivenom. Although that helped counter the [[coagulation|coagulating]] effect of taipan venom, it did not overcome the second effect of the taipan venom, which [[paralysis]] the [[nervous system]]. Though doctors initially hoped he would recover, he died the following afternoon. The snake, believed to be a [[coastal taipan]], died on 12 September 1950.<ref name="BT20140116"/><ref name="News19500801">{{cite news|url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article131128699?|title=Taipan "belonga devil"|date=1 August 1950|work=News|page=11|access-date=16 January 2014|location=Adelaide, South Australia}}</ref><ref name="Cushing">{{cite book|last1=Cushing|first1=Nancy|last2=Markwell|first2=Kevin|title=Snake-Bitten: Eric Worrell and the Australian Reptile Park|year=2010|publisher=University of New South Wales Press|isbn=978-174223-232-4|pages=53–54|chapter=5}}</ref>

==Legacy==
At the time of Budden's death, there were various rumours about the taipan, but it was not until Budden had captured this specimen that serious consideration was given to the potency of its [[venom]].<ref name="MP19500116">{{cite news|url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article109471733?|title=The Taipan - Deadly Snake on View in Renmark|last=Orrell|first=John|date=26 October 1950|work=Murray Pioneer|page=11|access-date=16 January 2014|location=Renmark, South Australia}}</ref> Two prior taipan specimens had been obtained in 1923, but those snakes were dead, and venom samples were contaminated.

Budden's captured snake was sent alive to the [[Commonwealth Serum Laboratories|Commonwealth Research Laboratories]] in [[Melbourne]],<ref name="News19500801"/><ref name="Cushing"/> where its venom was successfully milked by [[Zoology|zoologist]] [[David Fleay]],<ref name="TDB19500812">{{cite news|url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article63097255?s|title=Budden's Parents to Visit Grave|date=12 August 1950|work=Townsville Daily Bulletin|page=7|access-date=16 January 2014}}</ref> who was at that time the director of [[Healesville Sanctuary]].<ref name="Cushing"/> Venom from the captured taipan was instrumental in researching and developing an antivenom, which became available in 1955,<ref name="Williams2004">{{cite web|url=http://www.kingsnake.com/aho/species/extras/budden.html|title=The Death of Kevin Budden|last=Williams|first=David|date=January 2004|access-date=17 January 2014|archive-url=https://webarchive.nla.gov.au/awa/20110506020600/http://pandora.nla.gov.au/pan/107967/20110506-1206/www.kingsnake.com/aho/species/extras/budden.html|archive-date=6 May 2011}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> and saved the life of an 11-year-old [[Cairns]] boy before the year was over. The story of Budden and his sacrifice spurred efforts to capture other snakes and produce more antivenoms, including [[brown snake]] in 1956, [[Acanthophis|death adder]] in 1958, [[Papuan black snake]] in 1961, [[sea snake]] in 1962, and [[Snake antivenom|polyvalent snake antivenom]] in 1962.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://venomsupplies.com/student-projects/|title=Student and Post Graduate Projects|website=venomsupplies.com}}</ref>

In a 2014 article published in the ''Journal of [[Proteomics]]'', [[University of Queensland]], a venomologist, Bryan Fry reported finding [[Biological specimen|specimens]] of the venom harvested from the taipan that killed Budden. His study found that the venom had retained its toxicity after almost sixty years in dry storage.<ref name="BT20140116"/><ref name="Yong012014">{{cite web|url=http://phenomena.nationalgeographic.com/2014/01/14/80-year-old-vintage-snake-venom-can-still-kill/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140117225517/http://phenomena.nationalgeographic.com/2014/01/14/80-year-old-vintage-snake-venom-can-still-kill/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 January 2014|title=80-Year-Old Vintage Snake Venom Can Still Kill|last=Yong|first=Ed|date=January 2014|publisher=National Geographic|access-date=17 January 2014}}</ref>
